synopsis: Kalra and Paddock’s RAND report, dated 12 April 2016, provides the booklet’s statistical rationale for virtual testing: driving-only safety demonstrations require hundreds of millions, sometimes hundreds of billions, of miles, taking existing fleets tens or hundreds of years [f5464, f313, f5466, f9755]. Its benchmarks include 275 million fatality-free miles to demonstrate a fatality rate no worse than 1.09 per 100 million miles at 95% confidence, and about 11 billion miles to demonstrate a 20% improvement at 95% confidence and 80% power [f6922, f6923]. A 2019 conservative Bayesian analysis illustrates sensitivity to assumptions: a strong prior with 90% prior confidence reduces the 275-million-mile requirement to 69 million, while a weak prior raises it to 476 million [f6900, f6901, f6902]. The booklet says RAND’s statistical logic transfers to off-road machines, whose lower exposure makes field-only demonstration harder, but its numerical mileage requirements do not transfer because off-road claims concern detection and intervention per encounter [f314, f6664]. Staged encounters and thousands of simulation runs make the four-month plan conceivable, with rare-event claims requiring stratified testing, simulation volume and a credibility argument rather than customer-site hours alone [f14267, f14265, f14268]. There is an evidence-status tension: multiple chapters treat RAND’s conclusion as established, but the skeptic’s review says the report was identified as relevant without being verified in the research [f7400, f14268, f11203].
